title: Why Is the UK Still Failing Children Who Need Medical Cannabis?

content_html_sanitized:
The irony! From the beginning of cannabis prohibition, it has been justified by claims that it was protecting children from cannabis, but now it seems that the UK government is trying to protect cannabis prohibition from sick children.

It’s been nearly seven years since the UK government finally demonstrated at least some compassion by legalizing medical cannabis. But for the families of children with severe epilepsy, that promise remains largely hollow.

In 2018, two high-profile cases forced the government to act. Billy Caldwell’s life-threatening seizures returned when his CBD oil was confiscated at Heathrow. Billy Caldwell suffers seizure after cannabis oil confiscated

Then Alfie Dingley’s mother brought his case to Parliament, pleading for access to a medicine that worked where all others had failed. The resulting media firestorm pushed then–Home Secretary Sajid Javid to reclassify cannabis-based products for medicinal use. It was hailed as a landmark moment for science, medicine, and common sense. Medical cannabis: Parents 'denied it turn to illegal means for children'

Tragically, she just died: Cannabis campaigner was 'an inspiration and hero'.

And yet, in the years since, almost nothing has changed for the families who need it most. 'I break the law to buy my child's life-saving cannabis drug'

Legal? Yes. Accessible? Hardly.

The 2018 policy change was strictly limited to prescriptions by specialist doctors. But most NHS neurologists refuse to write them—citing NICE’s 2019 guidance, which rejected full-spectrum cannabis oil due to a lack of large-scale randomized trials. In theory, parents should be relieved that “pure” CBD (like Epidyolex) was approved for Dravet and Lennox-Gastaut syndromes. In practice, many children don’t respond to isolated CBD. They need small amounts of THC alongside it—a combination that only full-spectrum oils provide.

And so the cruel irony: the UK legalized the medicine, but only for those who can afford to pay privately. Most families spend over £1,000 a month to import treatment from the Netherlands or go through one of the UK’s few private cannabis clinics. As of 2023, just three children had received an NHS prescription for full-spectrum cannabis oil.

This isn’t science-based medicine. It’s cowardice, hiding behind the language of “insufficient evidence” while families go bankrupt and children suffer. We don’t require massive trials to approve rare disease treatments that affect a handful of patients—because the evidence, however limited, is often enough when the alternative is endless suffering.

What’s worse is that the moral clarity of 2018 has faded from public view. Once the headlines moved on, so did the political will. The Department of Health now hides behind NICE. NICE hides behind clinical trial standards unsuited to rare, complex conditions. And the children? They wait. Having seizures, often daily. Living with risks that could be mitigated today—if only our health system valued experience alongside evidence.

The families campaigning for access are not radicals. They’re parents. They don’t want to break the law. They just want to follow the science that really matters: their own children’s response to treatment. When private prescriptions work—when seizures drop from hundreds to a few a week—it should be impossible to ignore.

But ignoring them is exactly what the government has done. Legal reform must be matched by meaningful access. If NHS policy refuses to adapt, then Parliament must act again. Not seven years from now. Not after another headline. Now.

No parent should have to choose between their child’s health and their mortgage. And no country should congratulate itself on a medical breakthrough that only the wealthy can afford.

Let me suggest two searches on BBC.com.

First, search for “Cannabis for children with epilepsy”. There are numerous additional stories about families struggling to help their children.

Then do a search just for “Cannabis”. This will yield a seemingly endless number of stories about smuggling or illegal growers, often ruining rental housing. Cannabis prohibition in the UK is a disastrous failure.

See Cannabis use in the UK: a quantitative comparison of individual differences in medical and recreational cannabis users

Yesterday, I reported on the disastrous cannabis policies in Scotland.

So how is the UK doing overall?  “The UK had the highest rate of heroin use in Europe (out of 21 reporting countries). The UK had the highest rate of cocaine use in Europe (out of 26 reporting countries). The UK had the highest rate of ecstasy use in Europe (out of 25 reporting countries).The UK had the 4th highest rate of amphetamine use (out of 25 reporting countries. The UK had the 6th highest rate of cannabis use (out of 27 reporting countries.”

But they are doing a marvelous job of torturing sick children.
